---
title: "Async rendering"
---

Chameleon renders synchronously. In an async web app (FastAPI, Starlette, Quart, Litestar,
Robyn) that means a render runs on the event loop, and nothing else in that worker runs until
it finishes. chameleon-rs keeps `render()` exactly as it was and adds `render_async()`, which
renders on the event loop without holding it while it waits for data.

The framework integrations use it for you: an `async def` view decorated with `@template`
renders with `render_async`. This page explains what that does, and the opt-in extras built on
it.

## `render_async`

`await template.render_async(**model)` renders like `render()`, except that when a value the
template uses is awaitable (a coroutine, task or future), the render awaits it right there
and continues with the result. While it waits, the event loop serves other requests.

```{python}
import asyncio

from chameleon_rs import PageTemplate

page = PageTemplate("""\
<h1>${title}</h1>
<ul>
  <li tal:repeat="episode episodes">${episode}</li>
</ul>
""")


async def latest_episodes():
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)   # a database query, say
    return ['Rust for Python devs', 'Async templates']


print(await page.render_async(title='Latest', episodes=latest_episodes()))
```

`latest_episodes()` is passed unawaited. The render reaches `tal:repeat`, awaits it, and
repeats over the list it returns.

With no awaitable values, `render_async()` gives exactly `render()`'s output. That's tested
against every Chameleon fixture template and the render fuzzers, so switching a view from
`render()` to `render_async()` changes nothing until you pass it something to await.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Loading data in the view is still a good default

You don't have to hand coroutines to the template. Loading the data in the view (or a view
model) with `asyncio.gather` keeps data access in one place and makes the template a pure
function of its model:

```python
async def episode_page(number: int):
    episode, related = await asyncio.gather(db.episode(number), db.related(number))
    return {'episode': episode, 'related': related}
```

`render_async` still matters then: a big page renders without blocking the loop (see
[Offloading](#offloading-a-render-to-a-thread)), and the integrations need no change in your
views. Passing awaitables to the template is useful when a value is only sometimes used (a
sidebar behind a `tal:condition`), so it is never loaded when the page doesn't show it.
:::

## What gets awaited

Only an expression's **final value** is awaited:

| Template | With `episodes=load()` (a coroutine) |
|---|---|
| `${episodes}`, `tal:content="episodes"` | Awaited, then inserted. |
| `tal:repeat="e episodes"` | Awaited, then repeated over. |
| `tal:condition="episodes"` | Awaited, and the condition tested on the result. |
| `tal:define="items episodes"` | Awaited once; `items` is the result. |
| `${episodes.count}` | Not awaited: `.count` is looked up on the coroutine, an `AttributeError` as in a sync render. |
| `${len(episodes)}` | Not awaited: `len()` gets the coroutine. |

So pass the awaitable the template needs as a whole, or `tal:define` it first and use the
result:

```{python}
page = PageTemplate("""\
<p tal:define="items episodes">${len(items)} episodes, the first is ${items[0]}.</p>
""")
print(await page.render_async(episodes=latest_episodes()))
```

Async iterables (an `async def` generator) aren't supported in `tal:repeat`, as they aren't
iterable in a sync render either. Collect them in a helper first:
`[x async for x in source]`.

## Errors, macros and partials

Everything in the language works across a wait:

- **Macros and slots.** A layout's macro and the page's slot fills can await values.
- **Partials.** `${render_partial('shared/card.pt', item=item)}` renders natively, and the
  partial can await values of its own.
- **`tal:on-error`.** An exception raised by an awaited value is raised where the expression
  is, so the nearest `tal:on-error` handles it, as for any other error.
- **Cancellation.** Cancelling the task that runs the render cancels the value being awaited.

```{python}
async def broken():
    raise LookupError('the recommendations service is down')


page = PageTemplate("""\
<aside tal:on-error="string:Recommendations are unavailable.">
  <p tal:repeat="r recommendations">${r}</p>
</aside>
""")
print(await page.render_async(recommendations=broken()))
```

## Running helpers concurrently

By default the render awaits one value at a time, in document order. A page that calls three
slow helpers waits for each in turn. Two opt-in settings let them run at the same time. Both
change the order in which your code runs, which is why they're off by default.

### `@chameleon_rs.concurrent` helpers

Decorate an async helper with `@chameleon_rs.concurrent`, and each call to it written as a
whole `${...}` starts as a task. The render writes a placeholder and keeps going, and each
placeholder is filled in, escaped as usual, when the render reaches the end:

```{python}
import time

import chameleon_rs


@chameleon_rs.concurrent
async def fetch(name, delay):
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)
    return f'{name} ({delay}s)'


page = PageTemplate("""\
<p>${fetch('downloads', 0.2)}</p>
<p>${fetch('reviews', 0.2)}</p>
<p>${fetch('sponsors', 0.2)}</p>
""")

start = time.perf_counter()
print(await page.render_async(fetch=fetch))
print(f'{time.perf_counter() - start:.1f}s, not 0.6s')
```

A call runs concurrently only where its output can simply be written later: a whole `${...}`
in text, or one inside an attribute value. Anywhere its value decides what the template does
(a condition, a `tal:define`, `tal:content` / `tal:replace`, which may choose the default
content) or where the output might be taken back (inside `tal:on-error` or a translation), it is
awaited in place, like any awaitable.

If a concurrent call raises, the error is raised when the render reaches the end, in document
order, and the other tasks are cancelled. In a sync `render()` the decorator has no effect.

### Partials in parallel: `concurrent=True`

A template created with `concurrent=True` also renders its `render_partial(...)` calls
concurrently, when a call has an awaitable argument. Each such partial renders as a render of
its own, in a task:

```{python}
import pathlib, tempfile

folder = pathlib.Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
(folder / 'card.pt').write_text('<div class="card">${data}</div>')
chameleon_rs.configure(template_folder=str(folder))


async def load(name):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.2)
    return name


page = PageTemplate("""\
<section tal:repeat="name names">${render_partial('card.pt', data=load(name))}</section>
""", concurrent=True)

start = time.perf_counter()
print(await page.render_async(names=['a', 'b', 'c'], load=load))
print(f'{time.perf_counter() - start:.1f}s')
```

The integrations take the same setting on the decorator: `@template('page.pt',
concurrent=True)`, and `TemplateResponse_async(..., concurrent=True)` for Starlette's
`Templates`.

## Offloading a render to a thread

Experimental. `render_async(..., offload=True)` (or `@template(..., offload=True)`) runs the
render in a worker thread (the event loop's default executor) and awaits it. The render is
synchronous there, so awaitable values aren't awaited: load the data first.

- **On free-threaded Python (3.14t, 3.15t)** renders then run in parallel with the event loop
  and with each other. chameleon-rs ships free-threaded wheels and doesn't turn the GIL back
  on.
- **On a regular (GIL) build** it helps only pages dominated by long text, whose escaping
  releases the GIL. For most pages, a thread hop costs more than it saves.

## In the web frameworks

Every integration renders `async def` views with `render_async`, so all of the above applies
to the model a view returns:

| Integration | `async def` view | Plain `def` view |
|---|---|---|
| [Flask and Quart](flask.qmd) | `render_async` (Flask's async views, Quart) | `render()` |
| [FastAPI](fastapi.qmd) | `render_async` on the event loop | `render()` in FastAPI's thread pool |
| [Starlette](starlette.qmd) | `render_async`, and `await templates.TemplateResponse_async(...)` | `render()` in Starlette's thread pool |
| [Robyn](robyn.qmd) | `render_async` on Robyn's event loop | `render()` on Robyn's worker thread |
| [Litestar](litestar.qmd) | `render_async` with `@template`; `ChameleonEngine` (Litestar's `Template` responses) always renders synchronously | `render()`, in a thread with `sync_to_thread=True` |

Each module also has `render_async()` and `response_async()`, the coroutine versions of
`render()` and `response()`.

::: {.callout-note}
## A difference from the original libraries

chameleon-flask, fastapi-chameleon and chameleon-robyn rendered async views synchronously, so
an awaitable in the model was inserted as the object itself (`<coroutine object ...>`). The
built-ins await it. That includes test doubles such as `AsyncMock()` in a model.
:::

## Things to know

- **`markdown:` and other expression types** follow the same rule: the expression's final
  value is awaited. Load Markdown text before rendering rather than passing a coroutine for
  `markdown:` to convert.
- **A subclass that overrides `render()`** keeps its override: `render_async()` calls it,
  synchronously, so awaitable values aren't awaited. A monkeypatched `PageTemplate.render`
  (to time renders, say) counts as an override. See
  [Migrating](migrating.qmd#timing-renders).
- **`render()` never awaits.** In a sync render a coroutine in the model is just an object,
  as in Chameleon.
